summary.title: RxFunction Gateway Server - Baseline Threat Model
summary.description: Comprehensive threat model for the RxFunction W-200 IoT Gateway Server. This represents all identifiable threats without assuming controls are in place. Threats are categorized by STRIDE and mapped to confirmed findings (CF-xx) and uncertain concerns (UC-xx) from the security review.

threats.title: Manager User Identity Spoofing via Header Injection
threats.description: Manager app trusts useremail request header without binding to session state. Attacker can present different user emails while supplying a valid sessID cookie.
threats.mitigations: None in current code; relies on upstream proxy/ingress
remediationSteps: Bind useremail to req.session.user after authentication
Reject useremail headers supplied by client
Validate identity against server-side session before authorization

threats.title: Device Identity Spoofing in MQTT Messages
threats.description: MQTT message validation assumes AWS IoT policy enforces publisher identity, but code does not verify thingID against certificate chain. If AWS IoT policy is misconfigured or credentials compromised, arbitrary thingID can be injected.
threats.mitigations: AWS IoT Core certificate-based auth (external control)
remediationSteps: Verify AWS IoT policy restricts publish to device-owned topics
Log and audit device message origins
Add per-device topic validation in application layer

threats.title: First-User Bootstrap Creates Admin Without Approval
threats.description: When user count is zero, any presented identity is automatically assigned Admin Group. Attacker accessing empty database gets immediate administrative access.
threats.mitigations: None; relies on production pre-seeding users
remediationSteps: Disable implicit first-user bootstrap in code
Require out-of-band provisioning step or seed script
Add flag to prevent re-entry into bootstrap state after migrations

threats.title: API Key Compromise or Reuse
threats.description: API keys stored in MongoDB can be replayed. No key rotation, scope limitation, or rate limiting per key visible. Compromised key can provision systems without rate limit.
threats.mitigations: API keys are hashed, but no visibility into key rotation policies
remediationSteps: Implement API key expiration and rotation
Add per-key rate limits
Log all API key usage with context

threats.title: Write Routes Protected Only by VIEW Permission
threats.description: System and firmware mutation routes (setFleet, modifySystem, saveFirmware, saveFleet, saveGroup, modifyFleet) require only SYSTEM:view permission, not a write/edit/manage permission.
threats.mitigations: None; code explicitly checks for view-only permission
remediationSteps: Reclassify mutation routes to require edit/add/manage permissions
Review UserGroups and Permissions documents for actual role exposure
Add regression tests for permission enforcement

threats.title: Cross-Fleet Firmware Access via Identifier Enumeration
threats.description: Inbound device data requests are served by firmware_id or state_hash without verifying the requesting device's fleet assignment. Any device can request any known firmware ID.
threats.mitigations: None in application code
remediationSteps: Resolve thingID to system/fleet before serving firmware
Restrict manifest access to the active manifest for that system
Add tests for off-fleet firmware request denial

threats.title: Permission Hierarchy Bypass via Group Manipulation
threats.description: User service attempts to prevent escalation via permission levels, but complex hierarchy logic may have edge cases. User could attempt to add permissions they don't hold.
threats.mitigations: Permission filtering is present but not formally verified
remediationSteps: Add comprehensive unit tests for permission hierarchy rules
Simplify permission model if possible
Add audit logging for all permission changes

threats.title: Firmware Binary Tampering in Transit or at Source
threats.description: Firmware is downloaded from GitHub/GLG and cached to S3 without cryptographic integrity verification. Modified binary cannot be detected before device deployment.
threats.mitigations: None in backend; relies on device-side checks
remediationSteps: Persist expected SHA256/SHA512 digest with each firmware record
Verify downloaded binary against digest before S3 upload
Refresh S3 presigned URLs with verification on re-issue
Align with device-side signature/digest validation

threats.title: Manifest Tampering or Substitution
threats.description: Manifests are keyed only by state_hash and returned without integrity verification. Modified manifest file in MongoDB or S3 could be served to devices.
threats.mitigations: Presigned URLs provide transport security but not content verification
remediationSteps: Sign manifest records with server key
Verify signature before returning to device
Bind manifest to specific system/fleet to prevent cross-fleet substitution

threats.title: MongoDB Record Injection or Modification
threats.description: Application accepts user input and stores to MongoDB without full input validation on all fields. SQL-injection-equivalent attacks may be possible via document field manipulation.
threats.mitigations: Mongoose schema validation provides some protection
remediationSteps: Enforce strict payload validation at all input boundaries
Use parameterized queries (already Mongoose default)
Regular schema audits

threats.title: Session Token Tampering or Prediction
threats.description: Redis stores session tokens. If Redis connection lacks authentication or uses weak secrets, tokens can be read or modified.
threats.mitigations: Redis password in .env file (weak secret management)
remediationSteps: Use strong Redis password from secrets manager
Enable Redis persistence encryption
Monitor Redis access logs

threats.title: GitHub OTA Metadata Mismatch
threats.description: GitHub release asset ID is returned during lookup but not persisted. Download function expects ID but receives GitHub metadata fields, causing potential retrieval of wrong asset or failure.
threats.mitigations: None; code path is broken
remediationSteps: Persist GitHub asset ID in firmware record
Use asset ID exclusively in download function
Add integration test for GitHub-backed firmware end-to-end

threats.title: S3 Presigned URL Exposure
threats.description: Presigned URLs are returned to devices via MQTT. If message is intercepted or logged, URL is valid for configured duration and can be reused.
threats.mitigations: Short-lived presigned URLs (examined and found acceptable)
remediationSteps: Verify S3 expiry configuration matches policy
Enforce HTTPS-only for presigned URL delivery
Log presigned URL issuance for audit

threats.title: Session Tokens in Logs
threats.description: Manager app logs request details. If logs are not properly secured, session cookies or tokens can be extracted.
threats.mitigations: winston logger is configured but log sanitization not visible
remediationSteps: Mask or redact auth headers and cookies in logs
Restrict log file access to authorized personnel
Implement log rotation and secure deletion

threats.title: API Keys and Credentials in Environment / Code
threats.description: .env file contains API keys, secrets, and database credentials. If file is exposed or logged, all credentials are compromised.
threats.mitigations: .env not version controlled (per .gitignore), but checked in Docker/K8S config is unknown
remediationSteps: Use secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault)
Never pass secrets via environment variables in production
Rotate all exposed secrets immediately

threats.title: Firmware ID Enumeration
threats.description: Firmware IDs are sequential or predictable. Attacker can enumerate all registered firmware by trying different IDs.
threats.mitigations: None; access is gated only by thingID (which is not verified)
remediationSteps: Use cryptographically random firmware IDs (UUIDs)
Implement access logging for all firmware lookups
Restrict firmware visibility to enrolled devices

threats.title: User Email and Permission Information Leakage
threats.description: User emails and permission structures are stored in MongoDB and accessible via application queries. If database is compromised, full organizational structure is exposed.
threats.mitigations: Database credentials controlled via .env
remediationSteps: Encrypt PII fields at rest
Implement field-level access controls
Audit database access patterns

threats.title: Arbitrary Metric Fields Stored Without Validation
threats.description: Device metrics are stored with flexible schema. Attacker can inject arbitrary fields. Downstream systems may leak sensitive data if they assume trusted field names.
threats.mitigations: None in current code; schema is flexible
remediationSteps: Define strict metric schema
Whitelist allowed metric fields
Validate metrics before storage and consumption

threats.title: Rate Limit Bypass on Manager Routes
threats.description: Rate limits are applied but can be bypassed by rotating IP addresses or if upstream proxy forwards client IP incorrectly.
threats.mitigations: express-rate-limit middleware is configured
remediationSteps: Verify proxy trust configuration is correct
Implement per-user rate limits after authentication
Add CAPTCHA for suspected attack patterns

threats.title: SQS Queue Saturation
threats.description: Inbound device messages are queued in SQS. Attacker with AWS IoT credentials can flood queue, exhausting receiver capacity.
threats.mitigations: Poll speed and batch size are configurable
remediationSteps: Set maximum queue depth limit
Implement exponential backoff for processing
Rate limit by thingID at MQTT ingress

threats.title: Firmware Download Flooding
threats.description: Attacker can trigger repeated firmware downloads from GitHub/GLG by issuing many data requests with different firmware IDs.
threats.mitigations: Caching reduces downstream impact
remediationSteps: Rate limit device data requests per thingID
Cache firmware lookups to prevent repeated GitHub/GLG calls
Monitor GitHub/GLG API quota usage

threats.title: Database Connection Exhaustion
threats.description: MongoDB connection pool can be exhausted by rapid requests from many clients. No per-connection timeout visible.
threats.mitigations: Connection pooling is implemented by Mongoose
remediationSteps: Set connection timeout and idle timeout
Implement connection limits per user/API key
Add database query timeout limits

threats.title: S3 Bandwidth Exhaustion
threats.description: Presigned URLs are valid for duration. Attacker can trigger many parallel downloads from S3, exhausting bandwidth or incurring excessive costs.
threats.mitigations: Presigned URLs are short-lived
remediationSteps: Set S3 request rate limits per IP
Monitor S3 egress metrics
Implement CloudFront caching for firmware

threats.title: Admin Actions Not Fully Audited
threats.description: Manager app logs requests but not all admin actions (user creation, permission changes, firmware registration) are explicitly audited to tamper-proof log.
threats.mitigations: winston logger captures events but audit trail retention is unknown
remediationSteps: Implement dedicated audit log with immutable storage
Log all permission changes with actor, timestamp, previous/new state
Log all firmware registration and assignment changes

threats.title: Device Message Origin Not Cryptographically Verified
threats.description: MQTT messages are validated for format but not cryptographically signed. Cannot prove device identity to external auditors.
threats.mitigations: AWS IoT certificate-based auth provides some trust boundary
remediationSteps: Implement message signing at device level
Verify signatures in backend before processing
Log verified device identity with high confidence
